cards.author_headline: Pain Medicine & Phytoceuticals in a Digital Health Ecosystem
cards.post_text:
Spending two days working in “Gulhaven”, a simulated city created by RM Partners Cancer Alliance, DAC Beachcroft and Macmillan, was a powerful reminder of where healthcare needs to go.
The simulation brought together everything from mock GP practices and community hubs to a local cancer centre, placing people with lived experience at the heart of a two-day test of novel care pathways.
A few things particularly stood out:
The “Left Shift” is becoming a reality: Moving care closer to communities and reducing unnecessary medicalisation isn’t simply an ambition within the forthcoming 10-year plan — it is already being tested and designed.
Digital support and navigation: There is growing interest in digital care co-ordinators and technology-enabled tools to help people navigate increasingly complex healthcare systems.
The importance of being listened to: Perhaps the strongest message from people with lived experience was also the simplest: patients often don’t feel heard, and routine healthcare contacts don’t always provide enough space for people to explain what matters to them.

You don’t always need a complex intervention to make a meaningful difference. Sometimes, it comes down to listening, validating concerns, taking structured action and following up.
It was encouraging to see how community-based care and digital innovation are beginning to come together to create more person-centred pathways for the future.
cards.why: Healthcare simulation and digital care coordination discussion. Mentions following up and structured action.

options.text: The focus on digital navigation and following up is spot on, but the breakdown usually happens right after the interaction ends. When coordination lives in phone calls, WhatsApp and Excel, following up consistently becomes a manual bottleneck rather than a system. Digital tools only work if the operational handoff underneath is deterministic.

Patients feeling unheard often starts before they even walk through the door. When I called five clinics late at night for an urgent issue, three didn't answer, one played a robotic hours voicemail, and one had a language barrier. The sixth answered and got the booking. If the very first touchpoint fails, the care pathway never actually starts.

Digital care coordinators sound great in theory, but they fail at the edges like accents, names, and dropped calls. When building voice agents for healthcare workflows, you have to engineer the fallback path first, because speech-to-text will always mishear a patient on a mobile line. The model talks, but the deterministic code has to handle the rescue.

cards.connection_note: Hi Matthew, enjoyed your post on the Gulhaven healthcare simulation and the reality of the Left Shift. Your point about structured action and following up in digital care pathways resonated. Would love to connect.

cards.author_headline: Raising funds for CleverSkin / Director at Hypnotherapy Training International, CleverSkin Technologies and iMetaWellness
cards.post_text:
A medical product does not enter routine practice simply because somebody has shown that it can function.

In medicine, the more difficult question is often whether a new product can be used safely, understood correctly and incorporated into an already busy clinical pathway without creating new problems elsewhere.

Wound care illustrates this rather well. A dressing may be evaluated in terms of materials, performance and biological safety, but the person using it also has to understand when it is appropriate, how it should be applied, what to monitor and when the patient needs a different level of care.
This is where evidence becomes practical.

Laboratory and technical evidence matter, of course, but adoption also depends on human factors, workflow and the clarity of the intended use. A technically interesting product that is confusing to use, difficult to procure or poorly aligned with clinical practice may never realise its potential.

At CleverSkin, I am particularly interested in this boundary between technology and actual use. 

The useful clinical question is not merely, “Does it work?”
It is: under what conditions can the intended user use it safely, appropriately and consistently?

That question tends to lead to better product development as well as better medicine.

#cleverskin #advancedwounddressing
cards.why: Directly addresses clinical workflow integration and practical adoption, matching Rayan's medlog and discovery audit experience.

options.text: When I mapped a medical-logistics workflow supplying hospitals and clinics, the breakdown was rarely the technical quality of the items. It was the friction in the loop. 3,000 invoices matched by hand and weeks lost in procurement loops mean even a simple product gets stuck before a clinician ever sees it.

The step most miss before introducing anything new into a clinical pathway is mapping the existing administrative drag. When operations are already dealing with daily stock-out escalations and manual purchase loops, any new product inherits that chaos. It has to survive the current reality of the clinic first.

How do you isolate human factors and workflow friction during early product trials before scaling? In discovery audits, I usually find that the operational reality of a busy clinic exposes design flaws that laboratory testing never touches.

cards.connection_note: Hi John, enjoyed your post on medical product adoption and clinical pathways. Having mapped workflows across hospital and clinic supply chains, I resonate with your focus on human factors over lab performance. Would be great to connect.

cards.author_headline: Dentist, Independent Practice · Veneers, full-mouth rehabilitation and implant restoration · CAD/CAM and CBCT trainer · ThincClinic Rosebank, Johannesburg
cards.post_text:
DIGITAL DENTISTRY HAS CHANGED WHAT WE CAN SEE. 

Scanners. 
CBCT. 
Digital Smile Design. 
3D planning.
Same-day manufacturing. 

All of these technologies give clinicians more information. 

But better information does not automatically create a better treatment plan. 

A scanner does not decide whether a patient needs veneers. 

A CBCT does not decide whether a tooth should be preserved. 

Digital Smile Design does not decide whether whitening, alignment, bonding, veneers — or no cosmetic treatment at all — is the most appropriate answer. 

That still requires clinical judgement. 

At THINC, technology sits inside a broader decision process: 
HEALTH → FACE → FUNCTION → PRESERVATION → DESIGN → PRECISION 

The technology helps us see more. 

The clinical decision is what determines what we do with that information. 

Design the smile first. 
Choose the treatment second. 

— Dr Terence Moodley 
THINC
cards.why: Dentist discussing tech versus clinical judgment. Parallels AI decision boundaries nicely.

options.text: Exactly the same boundary applies in software. The LLM talks, but the code decides. When I built systems that handle sensitive workflows, the model provides the info, but deterministic code sets the rules. The tool sees more, but the architecture decides what happens next.

In the systems I build, the rule is the same. The AI assistant is read and propose only, and deterministic code commits every change. The model can suggest the path based on the data, but it never makes the final call.
When the digital scan and your clinical intuition point in completely different directions, how do you weigh the tech data against what your hands are telling you?

cards.connection_note: Hi Dr Terence, really enjoyed your post on digital dentistry and how tech informs rather than replaces clinical judgment. It parallels a lot of the architecture choices we make in AI. Would love to connect.

cards.author_headline: Implant Dentist | Entrepreneur | Dental Consultant | Anti-Aging & Wellness Technologies | National Anti-Aging Distributor | Nu Skin Partner
cards.post_text:
Dentists need to stop using revenue as the only proof that a practice is doing well. Because revenue can grow while stress grows with it.

The real questions are:
- What is your actual margin?
- How dependent is the practice on you being physically present every day?
- How predictable are your collections?
- How efficiently are your chairs being used?

And most importantly: Can your clinic run smoothly even when you’re not there?

A dental clinic is a healthcare practice, but it is also a business. And if the business depends entirely on the dentist being present, there is a limit to how freely you can live, grow and scale. 

I believe dentists need to build practices that don’t just generate more revenue, but create more freedom. Because the real goal isn’t just to make more. It’s to build something that works for you.

Follow my page for more conversations around building a smarter, more sustainable dental business.

#DentalPractice #DentalBusiness #PracticeManagement #Dentistry #DentalEntrepreneur #DentistLife #PracticeGrowth
cards.why: Dental practice owner talking about operational chaos and dependence on physical presence. Perfect fit.

options.text: When I had severe tooth pain at 11 PM, I called 5 clinics. Three did not answer, one played a robotic voicemail, and one had an Arabic-only voicemail. The sixth answered and got me as a patient. That dependence on physical presence shows up fastest when the doors close and the phone rings unanswered.
Call your own front desk at 7 PM or on a Friday. Whatever happens during that test is what your new leads actually experience when you are not physically present in the clinic.

The step most practices skip is checking what happens after hours. When the physical doors close, inquiries still land. If those calls drop, collections and chair utilization suffer long before the dentist notices the gap.

Total registered property sales in Dubai fell 12.5% year on year in the first half: 98,225 in H1 2025, 85,990 in H1 2026.

cards.post_text:
Nine months into the year, Dubai Land Department's figures put total transactions at Dh574 billion across 165,018 deals. That's already about 62% of what the entire 2025 calendar year did, Dh919 billion, with a full quarter still to go. On this pace, 2026 beats last year.

Dh379.4 billion of that is sales, the second-highest figure the market has ever recorded. The split underneath it is the part worth sitting with: ready homes did Dh196 billion across 39,320 deals, off-plan did Dh183 billion across 84,090, more than double the transaction count for less total money. Off-plan is pulling the volume. Ready is pulling the bigger checks per deal. Both are moving at once, which isn't what a market running on one story looks like.

September closed out at Dh29.66 billion in sales across 11,430 transactions. Business Bay topped every area at over Dh20 billion, with Airport City and Al Yalayis 1 right behind it.

I've been putting my own money into this market since 2008. Nine months of numbers like these don't move because sentiment is good. They move because enough people, at enough price points, decided the numbers worked for them individually. That's the kind of confidence I actually trust.
cards.why: Good market context for real estate, but lacks a specific operational pain point to solve.

options.text: When off-plan volume runs at double the transaction count of ready homes, the operational bottleneck shifts entirely to speed-to-lead. If an inbound enquiry sits for an hour while a broker is on-site, that lead goes to the next agency. Getting that first response down to under 10 seconds is the only way to capture high-volume markets without drowning the team.

The DLD numbers show the demand is there, but the hidden problem is what happens after the ad runs. When transaction counts spike like this, teams get buried in WhatsApp messages and missed calls. Most brokerages do not have a lead problem, they have a lead-waste problem between the initial enquiry and the first callback.

With off-plan hitting double the transaction count of ready homes, agents are dealing with a massive influx of smaller-ticket enquiries. How are growing brokerages handling that volume spike without letting leads slip through the cracks during peak hours?

“Waiting on the warehouse.”

Those lines feel polite on Friday.
By Monday they become three open loops with no owner and no next update time.

What actually works before the weekend:

1. Oldest open chats first — not newest, not VIP-only
2. Name an owner even if coverage is thin
3. Write the next update the customer will get (day + rough time)
4. If shipping or payment truth changed, say it before they ask again

Hiring more people to dig through unread on Monday is expensive.
Closing the loop on Friday is cheaper.

If you run ecommerce or CX WhatsApp in MENA:
what creates more Monday chaos for you — missing owners, vague promises, or silence after a status change?
cards.why: WhatsApp backlog and Friday unread messages. Direct match for Rayan's messaging on operational chaos and lead waste.

options.text: Relying on staff to cleanly close every loop before the weekend is a management hope, not a system. If keeping the queue clean depends on a human remembering to write down a follow-up time on a Thursday afternoon, it breaks by week three. The fix is structure that flags unassigned threads before the desk goes empty.

When coordination lives in WhatsApp instead of a proper system, the Monday backlog is only half the cost. The other half is the customer who did not wait until Monday and messaged a competitor instead. Vague updates and unread chats turn straight into lead waste before the week even restarts.

Closing Friday loops fixes the existing queue, but what happens to the inbound messages that land on Saturday when operations are closed? Do those sit until Monday morning anyway, or how do you handle the weekend gap?

Most Dubai property leads aren't lost on price.

They're lost on the second WhatsApp message.

A buyer asks, "Is the 2BR in JVC still available?"

The reply comes back: "Please share: 1) Buy or rent 2) Budget 3) Area 4) Bedrooms 5) Timeline"

On a phone, that isn't a conversation. It's a form. And buyers don't fill in forms.
The best consultants in Dubai never qualify like this. They answer first, ask one thing, and let every reply earn the next question. They switch to Hinglish for an Indian investor, mirror a Russian buyer who flips between languages, and know that 现房 and 期房 aren't the same thing.

I wrote down exactly how they do it:
- The 6 questions that actually qualify a Dubai lead
- How to ask them without sounding like a form
- Handling Arabic, Hindi, Russian and Mandarin buyers
- A simple Hot / Warm / Cold scoring model
- The moments AI (or anyone) should hand over to a human

This is also the exact behaviour we built into Reva AI, so it qualifies on WhatsApp the way your best broker would, not like a chatbot.

cards.post_text:
A company does not learn the strength of its Saudi operating model
when everything goes right. It learns it at the first service failure.

Market-entry plans often focus on launch: licensing, hiring,
workspace, partners, and sales. Far less attention is given to what
happens when delivery is delayed, implementation fails, an invoice is
disputed, or customer support cannot resolve an issue.

A practical principle from The Investor’s Guide to Saudi Arabia is
that market credibility is built through execution and disciplined
follow-through. When something goes wrong, speed, ownership, and
communication can matter as much as the original promise.

Before the first major customer commitment:

1. Appoint a Saudi-based incident owner with enough authority to
coordinate operations, commercial teams, partners, and headquarters.
2. Define an escalation path. Set clear triggers, decision-makers,
response expectations, and the point at which senior leadership must
intervene.
3. Build a recovery protocol. Explain how the customer will be
informed, how commitments will be documented, how root causes will be
corrected, and how lessons will enter the operating playbook.

This is not planning for failure. It is planning for trust.

A customer may accept that a complex operation can encounter problems.
What damages confidence is ambiguity: no accountable owner,
inconsistent answers, slow approvals, or promises that cannot be
executed.

Saudi market entry should include a service-recovery model
cards.why: Great post on operational failure and escalation. Fits agentic escalation rules.

options.text: When I mapped a distributor's workflow and built a multi-agent prototype from it, the entire design relied on deterministic, rule-based escalation. The AI handled routine tasks, but the second a discrepancy hit a specific threshold, it flagged a human. Escalation has to live in hard rules, not vibes, so the team only steps in when senior authority is actually needed.

The step most teams skip is designing the failure path for their communication channels. In the voice agents I build, we expect things to break at the edges. Phone lines drop or speech-to-text mishears an accent. Instead of letting the interaction fail, we build the recovery path first, matching transcripts to real databases and falling back to SMS if needed. If your recovery channel has no fallback, the escalation loop is broken.

Ambiguity is usually an operations problem wearing a communication costume. When I mapped a distributor's workflow, we found supervisors handling 50 to 60 calls a day just asking "where are you?" because there was no central system. When you look at local market entry, how much of the service-recovery protocol is left to manual WhatsApp coordination versus being hardcoded into a tracking system?

The toughest period in Dubai real estate since 2008.

Is the market dead? No.
Have prices collapsed? No.
Are investors panicking? No.

So why are well known agencies being sold?

This week I met a friend who owns a brokerage in Dubai.
He shared something you won't see in the headlines.

Two large agencies have just changed owners.
Big names. Years on the market.

Not sold because the founders wanted a new chapter.
Sold because they could no longer fund the business.

It took me straight back to 2022 to 2025.
A new agency opened almost every week.
Former colleagues left big firms and put CEO in their bio overnight.

Back then the market rewarded anyone who showed up.
Now it rewards only those who built something real.

Behind many famous logos today: unpaid broker commissions, cut marketing budgets, and no clear plan for what comes next.

A big brand is no longer a guarantee.
Sometimes it is a cover.

If you are a broker, ask your agency three questions before you stay:
When was the last commission paid on time?
What is the marketing budget this quarter?
What is the plan for the next 12 months?

If the answers are vague, you already have your answer.

I am building a team of 30 experienced, motivated brokers who win on skill, not on headcount.

AI tools we built ourselves.
Qualified leads every day.
People who know exactly what to do when the market gets hard.
